seo_description: Melissa kids' Christmas: the Melissa Tree Lighting Ceremony at Melissa Lake Park on Dec 5, with train rides, Santa and a drone show, plus town history.
lede: The story of Christmas in Melissa starts with the Houston and Texas Central Railway, which laid out the town in 1872, and with the Melissa Tree Lighting Ceremony, which began in 2023 and ends each year with a drone show. The fourth annual ceremony is Saturday, December 5, 2026, from 3 to 7 pm at Melissa Lake Park.
sections: A town laid out by the railroad in 1872

The Blackland Prairie soils and the Elm Fork of the Trinity River drew settlers to the Melissa area in the 1840s, when the Peters colony opened to settlement. The town itself was laid out in 1872, when the Houston and Texas Central Railway arrived, and families from the community of Highland, 2.5 miles north, moved to the new site. Melissa got a post office in May 1873. The Handbook of Texas says the name probably honors the daughter of railroad official George A. Quinlan or the daughter of railroad executive C. P. Huntington. Its population was about 100 in 1884 and had reached 400 by 1914.
The Melissa Tree Lighting Ceremony, since 2023

The City of Melissa called the December 6, 2025 ceremony its 3rd annual, so the tradition began in 2023. That year the schedule opened at 4 pm with a farmers market, bounce houses and a new petting zoo, then Mayor Jay Northcut read a story at 6:15 pm and the city tree was lit at 6:30 pm. The Melissa High School Choir sang, a friendly snowball fight followed, and a drone light show closed the night. In 2026 the fourth annual ceremony moves to Melissa Lake Park, and the city calendar lists train rides, characters, a craft station with the Melissa Public Library, hot cocoa and food trucks.
From the interurban to a fast growing city

From 1908 the Texas Electric Railway linked Melissa to the other Collin County towns and to Dallas, and before 1920 the town had electric lights, a telephone exchange and paved roads, unlike many rural Texas communities. A tornado struck on April 13, 1921, killing thirteen people, and a fire in 1929 destroyed many rebuilt buildings. The population fell from 500 in 1925 to 285 in 1949, then grew from 1,350 in 2000 to 4,695 in 2010 and 13,901 in 2020, with 16,983 listed for 2021 in the Texas Almanac. Families today can still ride trains at the tree lighting, and the museums below show what the interurban era looked like.
trains: Melissa was created by a railroad in 1872, and from 1908 the Texas Electric Railway, an electric interurban, connected it to Collin County towns and Dallas. DART's Red Line runs from Parker Road Station in Plano to Westmoreland Station in Dallas. For a train outing, the Interurban Railway Museum is in Plano, the Museum of the American Railroad is in Frisco and the McKinney Avenue M-Line Trolley runs in Dallas.

faq: How did Melissa get its name?

The Handbook of Texas says Melissa was probably named for the daughter of George A. Quinlan, an official of the Houston and Texas Central Railway, or for the daughter of C. P. Huntington, a prominent railroad executive. The town was laid out in 1872 when the railway arrived, and it received a post office in May 1873.
When did Melissa's tree lighting begin?

The City of Melissa called the December 6, 2025 ceremony its 3rd annual, which puts the first one in 2023. The 2026 ceremony on Saturday, December 5 is the fourth annual, and it is the first held at the new Melissa Lake Park on Liberty Way, according to the city calendar.
What does the Melissa tree lighting include?

The city calendar lists pictures with Santa and characters, a petting zoo, face painters, bounce houses, train rides, a craft station with the Melissa Public Library, storytime with the Mayor, live performances, hot cocoa, food trucks and The Melissa Market vendors. It ends with a drone show and the tree lighting.
Did an interurban train serve Melissa?

Yes. Beginning in 1908 the Texas Electric Railway connected Melissa to surrounding Collin County towns and to Dallas, according to the Handbook of Texas. That network made Melissa a commercial center for area farmers, and the town had electric lights, a telephone exchange and paved roads before 1920.

A tornado struck Melissa on April 13, 1921. The Handbook of Texas says it killed thirteen people, injured fifty-four and demolished many businesses. A fire eight years later destroyed many of the buildings that had been rebuilt. The Great Depression and mechanized farming then slowed growth, and the population fell to 285 by 1949.
